newsitem.title: USA: Jeans giant Levi Strauss to cut 1,000 jobs.
newsitem.headline: Jeans giant Levi Strauss to cut 1,000 jobs.

text.p: Jeans giant Levi Strauss & Co. said Wednesday it plans to cut 1,000 jobs -- one-fifth of its U.S. white-collar work force -- over the next year as part of an effort to trim overhead costs by about $80 million a year.

The cuts will fall on 20 percent of the 5,000 salaried jobs in the U.S. business of privately owned Levi Strauss, the world's biggest clothing maker. In all, the San Francisco-based company's U.S. business employs 26,000 people, most of them hourly workers.
Levi spokeswoman Linda Butler said management made the decision after a review of the company's U.S. business.

While the company's brands were very strong and the business was financially healthy, "we found overhead costs were not in alignment with revenues, they were rising at an unacceptable rate," Butler said.

"While we are exploring as many avenues as we can to cut overhead costs, it's really become apparent that we have to reduce our salaried work force in the U.S. business. Our estimate at the moment is that we would need to eliminate about 1,000 salaried positions," Butler said.

The company hoped to eliminate a number of the jobs through early retirement and attrition, but there will be some layoffs, Butler said without giving numbers. The company plans to cut the jobs over the next 12 months.
The company's goal was to "reduce overhead costs by about $80 million annually," she said.
"We sent out an e-mail to employees to alert them about the situation," Butler said, adding the next step was to explore the choices "and look at how would we do this in a responsible manner."
Departments that could be affected include finance, marketing, sales, customer service, communications and human resources, she said.
As well as U.S.-based workers, the cuts could also affect salaried employees in offices in Asia and Latin America that support the company's U.S. business, Butler said.
Butler said Levi Strauss again had a record year for sales in 1996. But she said increased competition was a factor behind the move to cut costs.
